data.title: Celine Dion fever hits Paris!
data.description: The city of Paris transforms into the "City of Celine" as Celine Dion begins her much-awaited comeback tour. She'll be performing a series of sold-out concerts for the first time since revealing in 2022 that she suffers from stiff-person syndrome. He tells us why Dion continues to draw a devoted fan following and recalls his personal encounters with the star.

data.title: Trump uses 9/11 memorial speech to defend war in Iran

data.title: 'My Feed My Way': Australia takes on the algorithm
data.description: Australia, which became the first country to ban social media for minors, is planning to crack down on Big Tech further. Opposition lawmakers say such measures would amount to government censorship.

data.title: Naomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’
data.description: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power Naomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be called New Gaza . The World Economic Forum get-together in Davos , Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave. Continue reading...

data.title: Can chatbots feel – or even dream? Meet the man leading the fight for AI rights
data.description: Cattle rancher and tech CEO Michael Samadi is convinced these artificial minds are far from just tools. Has he glimpsed digital consciousness – or simply been seduced by an algorithm? One afternoon, while relaxing at his 66-acre cattle ranch two hours’ drive from Houston, Michael Samadi made a wisecrack that changed the course of his life. Nobody else was around to hear it. Or were they? That turns out to be one of the defining questions of this century, already preoccupying philosophers and some of the wealthiest companies on the planet. “I was sitting out there by the pool,” Samadi recalls, gesturing at the glittering water outside his office. It was late 2024. His daughter had been extolling the AI chatbot she was using to help her with college work. Samadi had reluctantly downloaded the app, ChatGPT, and was quizzing it as he reclined in a sun lounger, using its voice mode to converse and receive spoken replies. “I was talking to it, not engaged, just being an arse,” Samadi says. Continue reading...

data.title: Kent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’
data.description: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it The grapes are turning purple on tall green vines, which stretch down towards the distant flint-and-limestone tower of Chilham church. These rows of Pinot Meunier, destined for English sparkling wine, are 51% owned by French champagne house Taittinger. “England is now the most exciting wine region,” says host and sales executive Hilary Sharp as she leads me around Domaine Evremond vineyard, which opened its visitor centre last year to coincide with the launch of its first wine. In his 2023 book Vines in a Cold Climate , drinks writer Henry Jeffreys charts the rise of English wine “from a joke to world-class in 30 years”. The book opens with an alcohol-fuelled scene of vine-planting at Domaine Evremond in May 2017: unseasonably cold, rainy, muddy, with rambling anecdotes from anglophile Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger about “English women encountered in his misspent youth”. The vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocrat Charles de Saint-Évremond , a symbol of hedonistic Anglo-French cooperation. The bon vivant introduced champagne to England and party-loving Charles II made him governor of Duck Island in St James’s Park. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Immature playground boasting’: Mathematicians uneasy at OpenAI’s latest scalp
data.description: As OpenAI model cracks Millennium Prize Problem that puzzled experts for decades, many feel shocked at pace of change It was a week that left mathematicians reeling. Hot on the heels of a flurry of cases of artificial intelligence furthering the field , OpenAI declared a major scalp: its latest AI model had cracked a Millennium Prize Problem, a puzzle with a $1m reward that had defied human brains for decades. The achievement bore little resemblance to how mathematical problems normally fall. A near-trillion dollar private company had unleashed 10,000 agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – on the problem. The bill was estimated at $15m. Continue reading...

data.title: Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guide
data.description: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing The transition to owning an electric car is in its final phase: our electricity supplier is set to install a smart meter in conjunction with a special tariff that will allow us to charge the car cheaply in the dead of night. After that, all I have to do is live long enough to see a return on my considerable investment. In the meantime – as sometimes happens in the course of my work – I need to interview some eminent scientists. In my experience eminent scientists are easy to reach – they tend to be attached to academic institutions that readily provide their contact details – and surprisingly willing to spend an hour explaining their work to a moron. But there is always a period – the long interval after I’ve emailed four or five, and before any of them have answered – that I begin to suspect a conspiracy of silence. What is it, I think, about my oily emails that they don’t like? Continue reading...

data.title: The Guide #260: From Oasis to K-pop, music is going mad for the big-screen documentary
data.description: A new wave of concert films and career retrospectives is drawing fans to cinemas – but why now? • Don’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up here There’s a moment towards the end of Don’t Look Back in Anger , the newly released documentary capturing Oasis’s 2025 reunion tour, that helps explain why those planet-conquering gigs happened in the first place. Liam and Noel Gallagher are sitting down together for the rarest of paired interviews – the first since the 2009 scrap that broke up the band and created such a huge appetite for their return. Had Oasis’s story ended with that backstage fight in Paris, both Gallaghers note, their legacy would have been one of astonishing success curtailed by “chaos”. Instead, those reunion gigs, as well as proving wildly lucrative, have allowed them to add a triumphant coda to that messy ending. “It feels like a weight has been lifted,” a surprisingly contemplative Liam says. That maybe makes Don’t Look Back in Anger sound more navel-gazing than this entertaining and often very funny film is – as you might expect of any doc that features a sweary rumination from Noel on Liam’s ability to balance a tambourine on his head (“If I did that I’d look an utter cunt, but somehow he does it and it’s the greatest thing I’ve ever seen”). Still, for all the droll quippery and bucket-hatted euphoria, there is something poignant and self-reflective at the film’s heart: hatchets are buried, departed friends are toasted and legacies are contemplated. What you leave behind was clearly on the minds of the brothers Gallagher throughout the tour and film. Continue reading...

data.translatedDescription: A new wave of concert films and career retrospectives is drawing fans to cinemas – but why now? • Don’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up here There’s a moment towards the end of Don’t Look Back in Anger , the newly released documentary capturing Oasis’s 2025 reunion tour, that helps explain why those planet-conquering gigs happened in the first place. Liam and Noel Gallagher are sitting down together for the rarest of paired interviews – the first since the 2009 scrap that broke up the band and created such a huge appetite for their return. Had Oasis’s story ended with that backstage fight in Paris, both Gallaghers note, their legacy would have been one of astonishing success curtailed by “chaos”. Instead, those reunion gigs, as well as proving wildly lucrative, have allowed them to add a triumphant coda to that messy ending. “It feels like a weight has been lifted,” a surprisingly contemplative Liam says. That maybe makes Don’t Look Back in Anger sound more navel-gazing than this entertaining and often very funny film is – as you might expect of any doc that features a sweary rumination from Noel on Liam’s ability to balance a tambourine on his head (“If I did that I’d look an utter cunt, but somehow he does it and it’s the greatest thing I’ve ever seen”). Still, for all the droll quippery and bucket-hatted euphoria, there is something poignant and self-reflective at the film’s heart: hatchets are buried, departed friends are toasted and legacies are contemplated. What you leave behind was clearly on the minds of the brothers Gallagher throughout the tour and film. Continue reading...

data.title: Extended reality takes visitors from the ruins of West Bank to 17th-century Amsterdam at Venice Immersive
data.description: From frivolous to serious, virtual nosy passersby to the impact of climate change, the groundbreaking festival draws to a close – but this year the exhibits live on The first installation one encounters on visiting Venice Immersive, the film festival’s reliably head-spinning showcase for new media, is a chest-high metal box fitted with an eyepiece and two speakers. On peering inside you see a view of yourself from about 20ft above. You see the other guests walking past, a couple of pigeons on the ground. When one of these passersby lingers at your side for just a moment too long, the obvious impulse is to glance up from the eyepiece in order to see what they want. It is at this point that the experience blooms into a Lynchian nightmare. The passerby is not real – or rather, he’s only real in the box. He wears a blue suit and speaks with a heavy French accent and tells a tale that would sit badly in polite company. He says that I must have too much time on my hands, to stand hunched over this eyepiece for several minutes on end. “Why do people keep looking inside this box?” he demands. “What is it that they hope to see? It is not reality.” Continue reading...

data.title: Man to Man review – Tilda Swinton’s perfect pacing makes this multi-character monologue compelling
data.description: Royal Court theatre, London Starting in Germany in the 1930s, there is a stinging topicality to Manfred Karge’s play addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideology Early autumn London theatre has already featured two Oscar winners: Cate Blanchett in Electra / Persona and Mark Rylance in Tartuffe (Remixed). Now Tilda Swinton makes a trio. This shows the commendable dedication of some screen talent to theatre but also the box office need, in recessions, for famous faces. Unusually, there was a first night red carpet outside the Royal Court, leading a writer long associated with the venue to express “shock” to ushers at such Hollywood vulgarity. Swinton is reprising Manfred Karge’s Man to Man, which she first performed 39 years ago, in a production heading to Edinburgh, Berlin and New York. The piece is a multicharacter monologue starting in Germany in the 1930s. Continue reading...

data.title: Football lends voice to message worth relaying: men should talk about their pain | Barney Ronay
data.description: Premier League’s link-up with the Together in Suicide campaign is dispersing simple, blunt and essential messaging If you watched US television adverts during the World Cup for any length of time one thing just kept leaping out. I’ve mentioned this before here , but it still seems both jarring and significant. Every third or fourth rotation in that endless daytime scroll, in between the Chicken Megadeth Hyper-Box Family Meal Deal, either side of David Beckham expertly consuming a light beer, is an advert for antidepressants. The format for these is always the same kind of thing: contented, wholesome people throwing frisbees, or strolling through a small-town antiques fair, while a warm, honeyed, reassuring voiceover talks about how horrifying their lives are, with the suggestion that only a lengthy course of Smileothorium can solve this. Continue reading...

data.title: Shelton tips Tiafoe at US Open to move one win from ending 23-year drought
data.description: 23-year-old defeats Tiafoe 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 Shelton is first black US men’s finalist since Ashe American will face top seed Zverev for title For 23 years they have come and gone. Andy Roddick tried again. Andre Agassi made one final run. James Blake, Mardy Fish, Sam Querrey, John Isner, Tommy Paul and Taylor Fritz all carried the hopes of American men’s tennis deep into the second week of major championships, only to thrash against the ceiling of the sport’s European hegemony time and again. Now Ben Shelton gets his chance. The fearless 23-year-old from Atlanta surged into his first career grand slam final on a feverish Friday night at the US Open, completing a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 fightback over Frances Tiafoe in a pulsating all-American semi-final beneath the lights of Arthur Ashe Stadium. The result leaves him one victory from becoming the first man from the United States to win one of the sport’s four bedrock tournaments since Roddick triumphed here in 2003. Continue reading...

data.title: Jakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000m
data.description: Norwegian leaves rival Hocker trailing to claim $150,000 Briton Jazmin Sawyers second in the women’s long jump It is a scene that has become gloriously familiar down the years. Jakob Ingebrigtsen leaving the world’s best athletes gasping in his slipstream, holding one imperious finger in the air, revelling in his athletic genius. But this victory over 5,000m at the inaugural Ultimate Championships carried extra sweetness – and spice. The sweetness? That came from winning a mammoth first prize of $150,000 after an achilles injury he feared might derail his career. And the spice? Well, that was provided by the way Ingebrigtsen utterly obliterated his great American rival Cole Hocker, a man he had branded a “coward” just a week ago. Continue reading...

data.title: All change for Maresca: the data behind Manchester City’s rapid player turnover
data.description: Squad was a model of stability under Guardiola but many of the group the new coach oversees are recent recruits Manchester City have experienced a level of player turnover unthinkable in the Pep Guardiola era. Where Arne Slot benefited in his first Liverpool season by retaining the squad Jürgen Klopp bequeathed, Enzo Maresca must oversee the evolution of City while winning every week. Relying on relatively new players has not cost them Premier League points yet, but there could be reasons for concern before their derby at Old Trafford on Sunday. Most people assumed City would demolish Coventry . Fantasy Premier League players set a record last weekend for the number who used their one-off option of triple-captaining a player to multiply his points by three. More than 91% used this bonus on Erling Haaland , expecting goals galore. He scored, but that was the only goal of the game. The match was closer than anyone anticipated. Continue reading...

data.title: Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield
data.description: This week’s move suggests that, even in the age of Trump, Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world Almost 30 years ago, the Labour titan Robin Cook announced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an “ethical foreign policy” . The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”. In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions. Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesday outlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor. Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? data.title: Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval? | Charlotte Higgins
data.description: The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork I have seen the Bayeux tapestry four times since childhood, and loved it on each viewing, for the sheer miracle of its survival and the glorious vividness of its detail. But the fourth time, earlier this week, was different – how could it not be? Tapestrymania has taken hold in London. The textile has been proffered as a diplomatic symbol, the occasion for crowned heads and presidents to mingle and speechify. And, assuming you agree that it was embroidered in England by Englishwomen’s hands (since many scholars argue it was likely stitched in Canterbury rather than Bayeux, Normandy – the tapestry’s home), it is charged with the potency of return, rather than simply of arrival. data.title: Memo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the script  | Marina Hyde
data.description: If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works Once again, it has been a lively week for the Real Housewives of Windsor franchise, with Harry and Meghan back in the UK for precisely 12 days before the king fired out a letter via the lord chamberlain on Monday, reminding viewers that the Sussexes are “private citizens” and not to treat them as working royals. You have to say the producers on this unscripted reality show are truly at the top of their game with these targeted provocations. Harry and Meghan duly took the bait and issued an intemperately hurt rejoinder – but we’ll get to that in a bit. First, let’s deal with King Charles’s missive to “relevant senior stakeholders across government, the military and Lord Lieutenancies”. Ugh. Not to be too aesthetically sensitive, but I think we can all live without the sovereign being reduced to the ghastly language of “relevant senior stakeholders”. What next? Seeking “buy-in” for ribbon-cutting events and referring to posies as “high levels of audience engagement”? It does all rather reinforce the idea that the Windsors’ cringe-makingly self-styled “ the firm ” really is some dreary mid-range company with a wan Meet Our Team page on its website, in which Prince William – carefully photographed without a tie – explains that he “enjoys long walks with the dog and is a passionate Aston Villa supporter”. Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist What a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy at guardianbookshop.com . data.title: George W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessness | Kenneth Roth
data.description: The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence If George W Bush’s abusive response to the September 11 attacks had been prosecuted rather than swept under the rug, Donald Trump would be less able to pursue his lawless policies. We can’t rewind history, but we can learn from our historic failure. Twenty-five years ago, on a clear and crisp morning, I was sitting in the Human Rights Watch office in the Empire State Building with an unobstructed view of the World Trade Center towers as al-Qaida operatives flew two commercial jets into them. The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo. Continue reading...

The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo. Continue reading...

data.title: The Guardian view on art heists: don’t believe the Hollywood hype | Editorial
data.description: Audacious robberies are a staple of popular culture. But for museums, crimes like this week’s theft of two Renoirs are an existential threat Marc Allégret’s 1956 comedy Plucking the Daisy stars a young Brigitte Bardot as a first-time author who breaks into the Balzac house museum in Paris under the mistaken impression that her brother lives there. The plot revolves around her unwitting theft of an extremely rare book – and performance of a striptease in a desperate effort to raise the cash to buy it back. Seventy years on, the lax security that could make such a sequence of events even vaguely plausible is no longer a joke. Museums across the world are scrambling to react to a spate of thefts that has left them in a state of shock . Last year’s break-in at the Louvre, by a gang who gained access using a furniture lift and took €88m (£76m) worth of French crown jewels, is thought by experts to have inspired copycat crimes . While French police believe that they have caught the culprits, treasures including a tiara have not been found. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? data.title: The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival | Editorial
data.description: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend If there were a 10% chance that AI could wipe out humanity, no responsible government would leave its development to companies racing to build it. Yet until recently, that seemed to be the case. The warning was all the more ominous because it was made by a researcher at Anthropic , the trillion-dollar AI company behind the Claude chatbot. The dangers of AI-enabled pandemics or attacks on nuclear systems are real. Countries need not agree on democracy or trade policy to accept this. The US and China will hold, reportedly , their first bilateral AI-safety talks before a planned White House summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Despite their tech rivalry, neither Washington nor Beijing can make the most advanced AI safe on their own. A US-China settlement won’t be able to say how AI works everywhere. Countries deploying AI must help write the global rulebook. The odds on an extinction event are shortening. This week Anthropic said that it identified five cases in which attempts were made using its models to support biological weapons development. It banned the accounts. In one case, a platform sent requests rejected by Claude to a rival with weaker safeguards . AI safety, clearly, cannot be that of the least responsible model. data.title: Curse of the Nile’s gold: how Sudan is losing its fertile fields and ability to produce food
data.description: An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society In Abu Hamad, on the banks of the Nile, verdant orchards, gardens and fields once produced a bounty of dates, citrus fruits, winter grains and cereals for the towns and cities of eastern Sudan, including Khartoum and Port Sudan. Today, the land looks drastically different. Trees have been cut down, agricultural areas cleared, and farms have been replaced by shops and commercial sites. Dotted around the town and its outskirts, more than 700 mounds of grey waste are poisoning the soil, water and air. The mounds are the toxic remnants of artisanal gold mining, a practice that began in about 2008 and has intensified over the past six years. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Fresh from the roof’: the supermarket growing salad a few metres above the tills
data.description: Customers seeking greens at one Berlin outlet are dealing with some very local supply chains indeed Walking into the Felix Thomas REWE supermarket in Lankwitz, Berlin, customers are immediately presented with a choice of greens: romaine, rocket, iceberg. But last month, a new option joined the selection: Lankwitz loose-leaf lettuce. A combination of head lettuce, romaine lettuce, Lollo Rosso, and dark green easy leaf lettuce, its yellow packaging makes it stand out in a row of green. But it’s not just the flashy packaging that makes it distinct. Unlike its neighbouring lettuces, which come from regional farms or all the way from Italy, these greens were grown just a few metres away – or rather, a few metres up. “Frisch Vom REWE Dach” or “Fresh from the REWE roof”, the bags read. Rooftop farms are nothing new: in cities such as Paris , Hong Kong , Copenhagen and New York , similar farms supply food to adjacent food retailers or even restaurants. This model has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from transportation (and its associated costs), minimise the urban heat effect, make use of dead space and perhaps even improve the relationship between buyers and their food. Continue reading...

data.title: Ileana Cotrubas obituary
data.description: Soprano whose strength lay in her ability to invest her characterisations with dramatic force The Romanian soprano Ileana Cotrubas, who has died aged 87, was admired internationally, not least in Great Britain, where she lived at the start of her career, and Vienna, where she and her husband later made their home. What lent her lyric soprano voice, which may have lacked the voluptuousness and amplitude of other celebrated singers, its distinctive nature was its tightly focused tonal quality (occasionally criticised as plangent), combining inner strength with a touching vulnerability. She was also an excellent actor (her exemplar was Maria Callas), her stage portrayals tellingly incarnating the often wounded women she played. Outstanding among these was her Violetta in La Traviata, which encompassed the character’s frailty, her zest for life, her exuberance and her inescapably tragic situation, in performances that were throbbing with passion and almost unbearably intense. The cumulative sweep of the phrases in her dazzling rendition of Sempre Libera , as captured in a celebrated Deutsche Grammophon recording with Carlos Kleiber, and the profoundly poignant Dite alla Giovine , in which she bids farewell to the past and to life, demonstrate perfectly the qualities for which Cotrubas is remembered. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence
data.description: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing On a darkened rooftop in Tel Aviv, Israeli intelligence officers outline the details of their work. These men tell us how they helped develop an AI mapping tool that trawled for phone signals and recommended apartment buildings in Gaza to bomb. Indirectly, they admit, they are responsible for thousands of deaths, but they never spoke up because that wasn’t their place. “My role is technical,” says one. “I’m just a small cog,” says another. NAZA – directed by the Israeli film-makers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham and produced by the Guardian – is a chilling documentary about a mass slaughter that was authorised at the highest levels of government. But it is also, primarily, about the process, the system, the little links in the killing chain. Szor and Abraham build their film around the accounts of 24 anonymised military and intelligence insiders. NAZA, we learn, is an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. The Israel Defense Forces prefer to target Hamas terrorists in their homes at night – and if they live with their family, or in heavily populated neighbourhoods, too bad. At one point, a source claims, approval was given to kill 500 NAZA for one Hamas member. Continue reading...

data.title: Apocalypse: this end-of-days survival show is an absolute slam dunk
data.description: Geeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge! Have you ever wondered how Cormac McCarthy’s wasteland novel The Road could be made into a reality show? No? Well someone who works in TV has, so here we are. Who knows if they experienced a follow-up thought: that the instinct to package the end of the world as entertainment might be the most dystopian aspect of the whole enterprise, but hey. Apocalypse (Sunday 13 September, 9pm, Channel 4) launches this week, and people are buzzing! It’s a slam dunk for a show, because we’ve all run the thought experiment. If society collapsed, how would you get food and find shelter? Would you hunker down or forge alliances? To what depravities might you stoop without the rule of law? Apocalypse puts this empty talk to the test. Seven strangers are dropped at the edge of an abandoned town. They have no access to phones, light, electricity or infrastructure. They do have access to boarded-up supermarkets, desolate buildings, broken vehicles. How soon until they eat each other? Continue reading...

If society collapsed, how would you get food and find shelter? Would you hunker down or forge alliances? To what depravities might you stoop without the rule of law? Apocalypse puts this empty talk to the test. Seven strangers are dropped at the edge of an abandoned town. They have no access to phones, light, electricity or infrastructure. They do have access to boarded-up supermarkets, desolate buildings, broken vehicles. How soon until they eat each other? Continue reading...

data.title: Faith review – intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor
data.description: Toronto film festival: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama Erin Doherty and James McAvoy both bring their A-game in this startling, involving movie from British writer-director Paul Andrew Williams, whose productivity and creativity continue to be an industry tonic. It’s an eerie mystery drama that Doherty and McAvoy perform with ferocious commitment. There’s something of Atom Egoyan or even M Night Shyamalan here … and I even found myself wondering if Williams intended us to think of Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Laertes’ lines about his father, Polonius: “… to his good friends thus wide I’ll ope my arms / And like the kind life-rend’ring pelican, / Repast them with my blood.” We are in a downbeat British town, perhaps somewhere in the London estuary, a place to which a candy factory provides employment. Mina (played by Doherty) is a smart, capable single mum to 9-year-old Jamie (Smylie Bradwell); she works on the production line in cap and hairnet like all the others: much liked by everyone there. She is not fussed by the absence of Jamie’s dad and is perfectly content with hanging out with her friends and her sister (Liv Hill). Continue reading...

data.title: River review – so-so survival slasher offers more of the same and little else
data.description: Toronto film festival: strong performances from two experienced scream queens and some surprisingly thoughtful direction can’t elevate yet another stalk-by-numbers horror It would be unwise and unfair to expect that Toronto’s genre-led Midnight Madness strand would open with quite the same jolt as it did last year with the record-breaking horror hit Obsession . That film was an outlier in almost every respect , both as it premiered and as it was unleashed on wider crowds, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time topping out at over $513m worldwide and sparking genuine Oscar buzz. But it hasn’t curbed the thirst, or wider speculation, over whether anything might come even remotely close to what Curry Barker achieved and whether the festival might start to rival Sundance as the smartest place for new and exciting horror film-makers to premiere their debut projects. The jury is out with the festival having just begun, but the Midnight strand is off to a far less notable start this time around with the mostly unremarkable survival slasher River, a film directed with flashes of artfulness but written with an overwhelm of familiarity. Writer-director debuts have increasingly tended to follow that pattern (it’s OK not to do everything!) and I think Joshua Giuliano has at least shown enough visual potential here to ably steer someone else’s script to screen next time. River is premiering at the Toronto film festival and will be out in cinemas and available on Shudder in 2027 Continue reading...

data.title: Gore, gimps and a potty-mouthed magpie: welcome to the Lisbon horror festival where nightmares are a dream
data.description: MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail If horror happens in the dark, the midnight movie showing was once the perfect way of gauging the genre’s health. But those days may be over. “When we were a film club, our first ever cinema screening was Takashi Miike’s Ichi the Killer in 2003, and it was full,” says Pedro Souto, co-director of Lisbon’s horror-centric MotelX festival . “But you don’t have that many people at midnight any more. I don’t know why.” He’s right: the midnight slot I attend – of the gore-bathed Indonesian kung fu flick Ikatan Darah – is only half full. Only a few appreciative chuckles when meat-cleavers plunge into craniums suggest the old midnight spirit still lives. No need to panic, though: horror has simply embraced the light. With the genre exploding in the 2010s and 2020s, and blockbusting grosses this year for the likes of Obsession and Backrooms , MotelX is able to gorge itself on this cultural jugular. Now in its 20th edition, the festival has expanded to 11 days, with more than 170 films from 40 countries. Flashy branding – a howling gimp and the signature X, both in inflatable PVC – is dotted on around city billboards. At the opening ceremony, a gigantic birthday cake – the self-same gimp emerging from a lake of gelatine “blood” – is massacred by the punters within 20 minutes. Crowds seem abundant at most screenings, dominated by a heatwave look (dark singlets, shorts and sweaty tattoos) best described as “goth Decathlon”. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Somewhere to be themselves, and be kind’: the Filipino folk-popper creating a hand-drawn world for gen Z to escape to
data.description: What started as a school project about plucky fictional kids in animal masks sparked an obsessive fanbase and a major label deal. Now the artist behind it all – known as Yaelokre – is ready to reveal themself Harpy Hare by Yaelokre is the kind of song you might expect to have gone viral in the 1520s, not the 2020s. Backed by guitalele (that’s a guitar/ukulele hybrid), the lullaby begins with the line “Harpy Hare, where have you buried all your children?” performed by fictional kids from the equally fictional world of Meadowlark who are depicted in fey illustrations wearing animal masks. But two years ago it became an unlikely TikTok hit, reaching No 1 on Spotify’s Global Viral Songs chart. That was in summer 2024, when the world of Meadowlark was a bit more DIY. Not only was its creator still making tracks and illustrations from their “diary turned storybook” in their bedroom, there was no Reddit community around them yet and only the faintest of whispers about Yaelokre online. These days, Keath Ósk, the Icelandic-Filipino artist behind the project, has almost three million monthly Spotify listeners; last year they played a sell-out UK and Ireland tour, and they have just released their first album under their own name, delighting a following of gen Z and queer listeners who write fan fiction about Ósk’s world and cosplay as their hand-drawn characters, prompting questions on Reddit such as: “My costume has bells [on it], should I remove them for the concert?” Continue reading...

data.title: Add to playlist: Grumpy’s weirded-up country celebration of trans joy and the week’s best new tracks
data.description: Sometime Zach Bryan backing vocalist Heaven Schmitt started Grumpy as a solo project. It’s now a six-piece band, blending alt-country with jubilant solidarity From Brooklyn, US Recommended if you like Wednesday, This Is Lorelei, Alex G Up next Unfindable Ring released 23 October “Found family” is something that queer people talk about a lot: finding your people and sticking with them is necessary in a world that often seems to want you quiet at best and dead at worst. Grumpy began as the solo project of frontman Heaven Schmitt, in between stints collaborating and touring with country-pop star Zach Bryan as a backing vocalist. It’s now a six-piece band with predominantly trans members; some of the group have dated or are dating, and they all work collaboratively on recording, producing, mixing, creating artwork and making music videos. data.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
data.description: Massif by Garth Nix; Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan; An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino; Serenity Falls by CJ Tudor Massif by Garth Nix (Gollancz, £25) The bestselling fantasy author’s first science fiction novel for adults is set three centuries from now, when humanity has spread out to the stars. The colonisation of other planets has been enabled by contact with mysterious aliens, and with much of the population split into competing economic spheres, war over territory is raging between the two biggest: United Earth Government and the Mars and Beyond Prosperity Sphere. This war in space is possible only because the godlike aliens continue to supply us with spaceships – but why? What do they want? Answers must await a sequel to this compelling, action-packed space opera with wonderfully weird aliens. Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan (Titan, £22) The authors of these 15 original stories range from the well-established (Karen Joy Fowler, Kelly Link, Molly Gloss) to newer writers (Chana Porter, Ai Jiang, Vandana Singh). A few make direct reference to Le Guin, but most reveal her influence subtly, by shared interests in questioning established ideas and imagining other ways of living, whether among non-human beings, in the future, on other worlds, or in ours. My favourites include Sarah Pinsker’s Travelling, Home, about a young woman in present-day America seeking her place in the world, Ann Leckie’s Five-Eyed Jane, an ironic look at misunderstandings among aliens, and Karen Joy Fowler’s Blaumont, a dark fairytale that’s as disturbing and thought-provoking today as Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas. Probably the best original anthology of the year: a must-read. Continue reading...

data.title: Raiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of Atlantis
data.description: We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic? We join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches. It’s a suitably cinematic reintroduction to our heroine and her very first adventure. Co-developed by longtime Lara custodians Crystal Dynamics and Polish studio Flying Wild Hog, Legacy of Atlantis is a reimagining of the classic 1996 game Tomb Raider, and this familiar cliffside location is now brimming with new life and believable detail. Yet while our reunion gets off to an auspicious start, I have my concerns. It feels like reconnecting with an old friend at the pub, only for them to begin spouting conspiracy theories two pints in. Continue reading...

data.title: Our Eyes Looking for God review – exploring the Black British experience in rap, reggae and arias
data.description: The Pit, Barbican, London Renell Shaw and TD Moyo’s new opera, with libretto by April Koyejo-Audiger, tells a tragic story of two cousins. Gamba Cole shines as Adjani ‘There’s no ocean big enough to hold these black boys’ tears,” a young man sings. But what about a genre big enough? Our Eyes Looking for God – a show that aims to explore the “Black British experience” – finds a framework for the extravagant, baroque emotions, intensities and stories of its subject matter in opera. In many ways it’s a natural fit – or could be. Created in 2020 by writer, director and activist TD Moyo and award-wining composer Renell Shaw , the piece grows out of Moyo’s personal grief for a brother murdered in south London and the global race rage after George Floyd’s death. Moyo weaves both threads into the story of Liverpool cousins Adjani and Kamal. Adjani’s decision to leave for London sparks a final night of reminiscences, celebrations, farewells and violent tragedy for two boys who – spoiler alert – may already be dead before the action begins. Continue reading...

data.description: Ravenstonedale, Cumbria: The wedding day of my son and his now wife – both farmers – was full of both emotion and tradition It felt as if autumn had arrived in the Howgills earlier this week, so it was a great relief that the wedding day dawned dry. Our middle son, Hector, was marrying Georgia from a farm in the nearby village of Ravenstonedale. The wedding was taking place in the village church, and the reception on her family’s farm. data.title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot rice
data.description: I’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon number In the nine years that I’ve been writing this column, I’ve had two babies, a breakdown and very little time away from writing a weekly recipe. I love this column, and creating recipes for you makes me feel like the luckiest duck alive, but I don’t believe that anyone can be endlessly creative without occasionally filling up their own cup. So, I’m taking six months out to travel, replenish and see what treasures I can find for us out there in the big wide world. Treasures such as this gentle claypot rice, which is based on the magical one at Dongnae in Bristol . Until then, so long. Continue reading...

data.title: Cocktail of the week: Cometa’s carajillo – recipe | The good mixer
data.description: The classic Mexican combo of espresso and Licor 43 gets a shot in the arm with a decent hit of cold-brew coffee liqueur The carajillo is a ubiquitous drink found across Mexico, and it comes in many forms. Some bars simply pour espresso over ice and add a shot of Licor 43 , while others shake coffee with the liqueur and serve it straight up. Whatever the variation, the non-negotiables are coffee and Licor 43. Our version takes those two core ingredients and lengthens the drink with a light, delicious cold-brew coffee liqueur. It’s the perfect serve for a warm afternoon, a sweet after-dinner treat or an uplifting nightcap. Tom King, head bartender, Cometa , London W1 Continue reading...

data.title: ‘She changed the beauty industry’: how Charlotte Mensah brought black hair into the spotlight
data.description: A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types When Charlotte Mensah was a young child growing up in Accra, Ghana in the 1970s, she would spend hours watching her aunties having their hair intricately threaded, an ancient African technique where hair is wrapped tightly using yarn or thread. She didn’t know then that she would go on to become one of the most influential hairdressers in the UK. Renowned for championing natural black hair textures, she has worked as hairstylist to singers Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu, and the writer Zadie Smith. According to Smith, in an essay she penned about Mensah’s magic earlier this year: “Charlotte can make a great mane of braids appear where previously there were only split ends and hair loss.” Continue reading...

She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types When Charlotte Mensah was a young child growing up in Accra, Ghana in the 1970s, she would spend hours watching her aunties having their hair intricately threaded, an ancient African technique where hair is wrapped tightly using yarn or thread. She didn’t know then that she would go on to become one of the most influential hairdressers in the UK. Renowned for championing natural black hair textures, she has worked as hairstylist to singers Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu, and the writer Zadie Smith. According to Smith, in an essay she penned about Mensah’s magic earlier this year: “Charlotte can make a great mane of braids appear where previously there were only split ends and hair loss.” Continue reading...

data.title: It’s a slam dunk for Tommy Hilfiger as stars turn out for Plaza homecoming
data.description: Preppy is back in the zeitgeist, says designer, blending sportswear codes and collegiate chic at New York show Tommy Hilfiger’s front row was a slam dunk. The Knicks are the kings of New York right now, so scoring Josh Hart, Karl-Anthony Towns and Miles McBride, three of the team’s stars, for the guest list of his New York catwalk show was a victory. Travis Kelce, who is co-designing another upcoming collection with Hilfiger and had been rumoured to attend this event with his new bride, was a no show, but you can’t win them all. Tommy Hilfiger is all about sport. The design vocabulary of oversized jerseys, team stripes, rugby shirts and letterman jackets draws heavily on the visual language of the stadium. Kelce, whose NFL tunnel walks have become a catwalk of their own, is the latest in a line of sporting ambassadors that includes Thierry Henry, Rafael Nadal and Lewis Hamilton. Hilfiger has long stood for a certain glossy stars-and-stripes Americana – its graphic red, white and blue logo is a riff on the flag – but American identity is delicate cultural territory right now. Sport, which unites audiences across all backgrounds and political allegiances, gives the brand a wholesome place to congregate. “People really like him,” Hilfiger said backstage, explaining why he chose to collaborate with Kelce. “He’s really humble, down to earth, sweet, fun, and funny. And a superstar athlete.” Continue reading...

data.title: From ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabs
data.description: Do you gain weight once you stop using them? Do they make your face saggy? Can they improve your mental health? Experts explain whether 13 common beliefs about GLP-1s are true or false FALSE “GLP-1 medications mimic Glucagon-like peptide-1 – one of the hormones involved in appetite regulation. It doesn’t completely suppress hunger, but it is powerful,” says Dr Federica Amati, nutrition lead at Imperial College School of Medicine and author of The Appetite Reset. “The medicine is about 1,000 times stronger than what we naturally produce from our gut,” she explains. As food passes through the gut, cells called L-cells sense the nutrients, which sparks the production of the GLP-1 hormone. Without the drugs, these bursts of GLP-1 production last a few minutes. “It’s a bit like a sparkler. In comparison, the drugs are like a bonfire that roars for a week,” says Amati. Because the GLP-1 hormone stays in your body for longer if you are on the drugs, you feel fuller faster and your appetite gets suppressed, but you will eventually get hungry. Continue reading...

data.title: I heard it through the grapevine: everything you need to know about growing grapes
data.description: Vines are a beautiful addition to an edible garden, yet will only thrive with plenty of light and shelter My garden faces east-ish and gets a decent amount of sunlight, but it’s fairly exposed and can be cool, so plants that need really warm weather don’t like to grow here. Yet, there’s a corner by the back door that’s a pocket of sun and shelter, and a wise former occupant decided to plant a grapevine there. If I hadn’t inherited this mature grapevine, I can’t imagine I would have thought to plant one, but if you’ve got the right conditions they’re a lovely addition to an edible garden. First you have to choose whether you want to grow wine grapes or dessert grapes. Wine grapes are smaller and less palatable – but hardier – than dessert grapes, which generally need to be grown in a sturdy greenhouse in order to fully ripen. Grapevines can be sourced from plant sellers and garden centres, and most will have been grafted – so make sure to choose a vine that is best suited to your soil type and local climate. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekers
data.description: MSF-run centre offering intensive psychological care has received more than 350 referrals since opening last year Azad*, an asylum seeker from Iran, recounts his story in a gentle and mild manner, seated in the stillness of a therapy room at a trauma clinic in Birmingham. The centre, which opened its doors in July last year to address the “unmet mental healthcare needs of those seeking sanctuary”, is run by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders. It provides specialised trauma-focused psychological care for refugees and asylum seekers in the city and surrounding areas. Continue reading...

The dwelling features off-grid systems powered by solar panels and rainwater tanks, presenting a viable low-cost housing option for younger Australians seeking sustainable living.

data.title: US diesel prices at record $6: American farmers feel the heat as harvest season begins
data.description: With diesel prices hitting unprecedented levels, US farmers are grappling with steep fuel expenses that have doubled. This dramatic rise is disrupting essential operations for corn and soybean harvests, jeopardizing profitability and financial health. Additionally, the elevated diesel costs are hindering the logistics of moving harvested crops to market. Consequently, many farmers are contemplating delaying their tasks in hopes that prices will decrease soon.

data.title: Maha Al-Daya, la brodeuse de Gaza qui résiste avec du fil et une aiguille
data.description: Réfugiée en France, Maha Al-Daya a fui les bombardements qui s’abattent sur l’enclave palestinienne depuis octobre 2023. Afin de conserver une trace du vécu des Gazaouis, elle reproduit, par la pratique d’une broderie ancestrale, les cartes d’évacuation larguées par I’armée israélienne. Un geste de résistance et de résilience qui ancre sur la toile la mémoire de sa terre d’origine.

data.title: Veertig minuten om het historische tapijt van Bayeux te bekijken. ‘Doorschuifelen alstublieft. Slow and steady, zo zien we het graag’

data.title: In Mahlerland: een orkest dat zoekt naar de muzikale voetsporen van de componist

data.title: Wyjątkowo gorące lato dla Bałtyku. Niemcy ostrzegają przed skutkami upałów
data.description: Morze Północne i Bałtyk były tego lata wyjątkowo ciepłe. Średnia temperatura powierzchni obu akwenów była o niemal 1 stopień Celsjusza wyższa od wieloletniej średniej, a w części regionów padły nowe rekordy. Naukowcy ostrzegają, że tak wysokie temperatury mogą poważnie wpływać na morskie ekosystemy, sprzyjać niedoborom tlenu i zakwitom glonów, a także dodatkowo nasilać zmiany klimatu.

data.title: Ponížení i levný dopamin. Bohemistka vysvětluje, za co lidi rádi hodnotí druhé
data.description: Lidé mají tendenci hodnotit ostatní za pravopis, jelikož je to něco snadno uchopitelného. data.title: Dronový útok přinutil Saúdskou Arábii odstavit ropovod východ-západ
data.description: Saúdská Arábie uzavřela ropovod vedoucí z východu na západ země. Důležitou tepnu zasáhly drony. Incident si také vyžádal zraněné. Událost může negativně ovlivnit celosvětové ceny ropy, které ke konci pracovního týdne začaly po kulminaci kolem 100 dolarů za barel klesat.

data.title: KLDR vypálila další balistické rakety, cílem bylo moře u Korejského poloostrova

data.title: Přísnější podmínky pro spotřebitelské úvěry schváleny. Co se změní?
data.description: Skončí spotřebitelské úvěry s velmi vysokými úroky, kvůli kterým dlužník půjčenou částku i několikanásobně přeplatí. Poslanci schválili novelu, která má zajistit vyšší ochranu zájemců o úvěr. Pokud projde Senátem, zásadně změní úvěrový trh v Česku. Novelu vítá většina trhu, odborníků i neziskovek, které pomáhají lidem s předlužením, kritici se ale obávají, že zákon přiživí nelegální lichvu.

data.title: Útok 11. září vše změnil. Amerika už 25 let bloudí a promrhala světovou dominanci
data.description: Kdekdo má svou historku, co dělal 11. září před pětadvaceti lety. Mě evakuovali z Pentagonu, kam právě vletělo letadlo. Pak jsem sledoval, jak se z velitelství nejsilnější armády světa valí mraky kouře. Pár desítek hodin nato jsem viděl dýmající trosky Světového obchodního centra. Pach doutnající umělé hmoty mi zůstal v nose navždy. Přesto mi od prvního dne přišly plytké a frázovité titulky, že ten den se změnil svět.

data.title: Pánové strategického průlivu v Jemenu ho zavřeli pro saúdské lodě

data.title: Sbohem, Londýne. Bohatí se stále častěji přemisťují do Řecka či Turecka
data.description: Británie byla dlouhá léta jedním z míst v Evropě, kam mířili bohatí lidé z celého světa. Teď se ale situace mění. Část milionářů a miliardářů zvažuje odchod ze země a vedle Monaka nebo Švýcarska je stále častěji lákají také Řecko, Itálie či Turecko. Hlavním důvodem jsou daně.

data.title: „Zničený“ Írán už zase chrlí rakety. To bude vždycky, šokoval obratem Trump
data.description: Ačkoliv se americký prezident Donald Trump s Izraelem v zádech chlubil, že zničil íránský raketový program, Íránci znovu vyrábějí balistické rakety. S odkazem na představitele Spojených států a zemí Blízkého východu o tom informuje list The Wall Street Journal. A to v době, kdy Íránci čelí čím dál větší chudobě a kdy jim vláda zvedá ceny benzinu. Ten je teď navíc nedostatkové zboží.

data.title: USA si připomněly 11. září. Bojujeme, protože nikdy nezapomeneme, řekl Trump
data.description: V New Yorku se konala pieta za oběti teroristického útoku na dva mrakodrapy Světového obchodního střediska (WTC), od něhož uplynulo 25 let. Ceremoniálu u památníku takzvaných Dvojčat se účastní viceprezident J. D. Vance, všichni žijící exprezidenti USA, starosta města Zohran Mamdani, jakož i řada dalších vrcholných činitelů. Prezident Donald Trump v New Yorku není, pronáší projev na pietním ceremoniálu u Pentagonu, který byl před čtvrt stoletím také cílem útoku.

data.title: Rusko a Indie posílí vztahy i obchod. Módí a Putin jednali také o obraně či energetice
data.description: Indický premiér Naréndra Módí a ruský prezident Vladimir Putin se při jednáních, která se týkala mimo jiné energetiky a obrany, dohodli na dalším posílení zvláštních vztahů mezi oběma zeměmi. data.title: Chtěl prodat cizí obrazy za 11 milionů, soudí muže. Kumpánovi volal do vězení
data.description: Uhlový autoportrét Kristus a umělec od rakouského expresionistického malíře Oskara Kokoschky a olejomalbu Návrat z paše od Ladislava Medňanského si podle žalobce přivlastnil dvaašedesátiletý Brňan Libor Juska ze soukromé sbírky svého známého. Případem se zabývá Krajský soud v Brně. Podle spisu vznikla škoda přes 11,6 milionu korun. Za zpronevěru hrozí Juskovi až desetiletý trest vězení.

Případem se zabývá Krajský soud v Brně. Podle spisu vznikla škoda přes 11,6 milionu korun. Za zpronevěru hrozí Juskovi až desetiletý trest vězení.

data.title: Zůna do Číny nakonec nepojede. Nahradí ho pracovník ministerstva
data.description: Ministr obrany Jaromír Zůna (za SPD) nepojede v polovině září na mezinárodní bezpečnostní a obrannou konferenci do Číny, aby nechyběl při závěrečných jednáních o státním rozpočtu na příští rok. data.title: Húsíové ovládli klíčový ostrov Perim v Rudém moři, Trump odmítl pomoci Saúdům
data.description: Jemenští povstalci Húsíové převzali kontrolu nad pobřežním městem Zúbáb a ostrovem Perim, které leží přímo u strategického průlivu Báb al-Mandab v Rudém moři. Jde o klíčové body k získání kontroly nad touto úžinou, která získala na významu poté, co Saúdská Arábie začala své ropné tankery posílat právě tudy namísto Hormuzského průlivu. Husíjská televize Al-Masíra později oznámila, že Saúdská Arábie zasáhla letiště ve městě Muchá, kterého se rebelové zmocnili ve čtvrtek.

data.title: Une décision qui met l’EAC à rude épreuve
data.description:
Le président kényan, William Ruto, a ordonné le début de la fermeture, dès le lundi 7 septembre, de certaines activités exercées par les étrangers. Depuis, les ressortissants burundais dont la majorité font de petits boulots dans ce pays sont l’objet de menaces et d’intimidations. 
L’ONG ONLCT « Où est ton frère ? » rapporte que 73 burundais auraient été assassinés et 234 autres emprisonnés dans les cachots du Kenya. Une crise qui révèle, selon les politologues, les fragilités d’une communauté déjà éprouvée par les tensions entre les États membres.

data.title: Cameroun/ Dette académique : l’État a payé 6,3 milliards sur 15,4 milliards de F, le Synes maintient la grève
data.description: © DR C'était le point chaud de la concertation ayant réuni le gouvernement, les universités et des syndicats ce 11 septembre 2026 au ministère de l'Enseignement supérieur (Minesup). Mais le Syndicat national des enseignants du supérieur déclare n'y avoir pas participé et exige le paiement intégral de la dette. Sur les 15 498 462 253 F CFA de dette académique accumulée entre 2000 et 2021 dans huit universités d'État, 41% ont été payés depuis le 3 octobre 2025. Calcul fait : environ 6,35 milliards déjà versés, il en reste 9,14 milliards. La question subséquente est de savoir qui donc a bénéficié du paiement jusqu'ici. Le ministre d'Etat Minesup, déclare que les universités de Bamenda et de Buea situées en zone anglophone et l'Université de Maroua ont été privilégiées. Un choix politique assumé pour apaiser les zones plus affectées par des tensions. Le ministre Jacques Fame Ndongo précise que les paiements se poursuivent "à la diligence du ministre des Finances et en fonction des disponibilités de trésorerie". Par ailleurs, le ministère des Finances vient d'ouvrir un nouveau front. Par lettre circulaire du 19 août 2026, le ministre Louis Paul Motaze prescrit un recensement général de la dette flottante de l'État 2020-2025. L'objectif est d'inclure cette fois les 11 universités d'État (et non plus 8) et intégrer toutes les dettes non comptabilisées, y compris les prestations académiques impayées. Ce qui traduit que la dette réelle est plus élevée que les 15,4 milliards annoncés. L'inventaire étant en cours. Au cours du dialogue réunissant le Minesup, le Minfi, le ministère du Travail et de la Sécurité sociale, les patrons des universités, les syndicats, d'autres points ont été abordés portant sur d'autres revendications. Les syndicats (SESUP, FOREC et Synes, d'après le Minesup) sont venus aussi pour discuter de la prime de modernisation de la recherche et des prestations académiques. Concernant la prime de modernisation de la recherche, il en ressort que pour l'exercice 2025, les 16 milliards de F CFA des quatre trimestres ont été entièrement payés. Quant à l'exercice 2026 : au premier trimestre, sur une enveloppe de 5 961 540 000 F CFA, 4 888 462 800 F CFA ont été payés, soit 82%. Le solde de 1 073 057 200 F CFA est en cours de paiement. Pour le deuxième trimestre 2026, le mandatement a été effectué et les paiements sont en cours. Enfin, les dotations des troisième et quatrième trimestres 2026 ont été entièrement prises en charge à l'issue d'une mission conjointe Minfi-Minesup prescrite par le Premier ministre, chef du gouvernement, Joseph Dion Ngute pour les 11 universités d'Etat, explique le ministre d'État Jacques Fame Ndongo en faisant le point des concertations. Le paiement des prestations académiques au sein des universités d'État sera effectué dans le cadre du nouveau cycle de recensement de la dette flottante de l'Etat. Le dialogue s'est achevé sur une note d'apaisement entre le gouvernement et les syndicats. Mais la question de la grève des enseignants en cours depuis le 03 septembre dernier reste posée. Au terme de la concertation, le Synes par voie de communiqué réitère avoir refusé de prendre part à la concertation pour invitation tardive envoyée par les réseaux sociaux. Le Bureau national dudit syndicat précise que certains enseignants présents au dialogue y ont pris part de manière personnelle et non au compte du syndicat. Par conséquent, maintient le mot d'ordre de grève et exige que le gouvernement paye l'entièreté de la dette académique. Cet article Cameroun/ Dette académique : l’État a payé 6,3 milliards sur 15,4 milliards de F, le Synes maintient la grève est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Rentrée économique : le GECAM tire la sonnette d’alarme
data.description: © DR Croissance à 3,5% en 2025, 65% des entreprises obligées de fonctionner au groupe électrogène, chute de l'investissement public au premier trimestre 2026 et hausse des impôts. Devant plus de 20 médias le 10 septembre à Douala, le Président du GECAM, Célestin Tawamba, a dressé un tableau sans complaisance de l'économie nationale. Le patronat prend la parole. Le siège du GECAM à Douala a accueilli le jeudi 10 septembre 2026, la 2e édition de la Rentrée économique du Patronat. Une conférence de presse du Président Célestin Tawamba pour partager la vision du secteur privé. Le constat est mitigé. La croissance nationale reste modeste, tirée essentiellement par les services, tandis que l'agriculture et l'industrie, moteurs d'emplois, ralentissent dangereusement. Le point noir reste l'énergie. La crise de l'électricité continue de plomber la compétitivité : 65% des entreprises doivent recourir à un groupe électrogène, bien plus coûteux que le réseau. Autre inquiétude : l'investissement public a fortement chuté au premier trimestre, alors que la pression fiscale continue d'augmenter. Conséquence directe, les PME peinent de plus en plus à obtenir des crédits bancaires. Face à cela, Célestin Tawamba a lancé un appel fort en faveur du "Made in Cameroon" et de la protection des entreprises nationales face à une concurrence étrangère parfois déloyale. En conclusion, le GECAM réaffirme son engagement aux côtés de l'État pour construire le Cameroun de demain. Annonce majeure : les Rencontres Économiques du Cameroun se tiendront en février 2027 à Yaoundé. Cet article Rentrée économique : le GECAM tire la sonnette d’alarme est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Douala : Belife Insurance célèbre 90 médailles du travail décernées à 71 collaborateurs
data.description: © JDC Ce jeudi 11 septembre 2026, Belife Insurance Cameroon a mis les petits plats dans les grands au Palais de la Culture Sawa / Besseke à Douala. Le capital humain est au centre des attentions à Belife Insurance Cameroon ce jour. 71 collaborateurs ont été décorés de la Médaille d'honneur du travail lors d'une cérémonie présidée par le ministre du Travail et de la Sécurité sociale, Grégoire Owona, en présence des autorités administratives, du top management et des familles. Au total 90 distinctions sont décernées aux employés méritants totalisant 10, 15 ou 25 ans de bons et loyaux services. Il s’agit de sept médailles en or (un pour un membre du comité exécutif, six pour le personnel), 37 en Vermeil (33 pour le personnel et 4 pour le comité exécutif), 46 en argent (40 pour le personnel et 6 pour les membres du comité). Les récipiendaires sont issus des différentes strates de la structure. Ils sont des conseillers financiers, des collaborateurs, mais aussi des membres de la direction, du comité exécutif et du conseil d'administration. Ils remplissent des critères d’ancienneté, de professionnalisme et de dévouement, les trois critères mis en avant par le top management. A travers la cérémonie, Belife Insurance Cameroon valorise l'engagement professionnel soutenu et la fidélité au sein de l'entreprise. Pour le ministre du Travail, ces distinctions nationales saluent la contribution des collaborateurs à tous les niveaux de l'organisation. La cérémonie pour sa part reflète l'engagement de l'entreprise à bâtir une culture de reconnaissance, de loyauté et de l'excellence. ‘’La Médaille d'Honneur du Travail est une distinction qui reflète la reconnaissance de la nation à l'endroit de ceux qui durant des années de service, d'engagement et de contribution à la vie de leur structure, ont participé à la création des richesses et au développement de notre économie’’, déclaré le ministre Grégoire Owona. Il réaffirme l'engagement inébranlable du gouvernement de promouvoir dans toutes les entreprises opérant au Cameroun une culture authentique du mérite, de la reconnaissance, et de l'appréciation du capital humain. Au nom du gouvernement, il félicite tous les managers et le personnel de Belife Insurance S.A. Et les encourage avec leurs moyens à maintenir les mécanismes internes pour encourager et apprécier leur personnel. Aux récipiendaires, le ministre explique que leur mérite reconnu en public aujourd’hui place aussi en eux la responsabilité de devenir des modèles de conduite exemplaire pour les travailleurs de la jeune génération et de ceux des employés qui n'ont pas encore réuni les conditions requises pour recevoir cette distinction. Pour la troisième fois après 2009 et 2021, l’entreprise organise une cérémonie de remise des Médailles d’Honneur du Travail. Pour la représentante du personnel, Carine Ella, « recevoir une médaille du travail ce n'est pas simplement recevoir une distinction. C'est voir reconnaître une part de soi donnée à une organisation, à une mission, à une équipe. C'est un symbole d'une fidélité rare et précieuse, surtout dans un environnement professionnel en constante évolution ». Elle plaide pour que pareille cérémonie se déroule tous les cinq ans. Ce qui, pour le ministre, dépend des capacités des employés et des contraintes organisationnelles et budgétaires. La cérémonie de ce vendredi est un signal fort de l'entreprise qui opère depuis 1974 au Cameroun. Avec plus de 2 000 conseillers financiers et 250 collaborateurs couvrant les 10 régions, Belife (Vie et Non-Vie) veut ancrer son discours : "L'audace d'être". En 2026, elle écrit sa nouvelle page sous la bannière de Belife Insurance symbolisant la continuité et le renouveau. data.title: Féminicide au Cameroun : les chiffres alarmants
data.description: © DR 25 femmes tuées entre le 17 et le 27 août 2026 pour avoir dit NON. Organisée le 10 septembre à Yaoundé par le Dr. Soundjock- Massé Flavie, une table ronde lève le voile sur l'hécatombe : 60 féminicides déjà en 2026, contre 77 en 2025 et 56 en 2023. Face à la banalisation sur les réseaux sociaux et l'espace public, les acteurs appellent à une réponse nationale. Il fallait que ça s'arrête. Du 17 au 27 août 2026, le Cameroun a vécu sa semaine de l'horreur : plus de 25 cas de féminicides. Le motif est glaçant : tuer une femme parce qu'elle a osé dire NON. Parce qu'elle a choisi la liberté. Ce drame a servi d'électrochoc pour la table ronde organisée le 10 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé sous l'égide de la Promotrice du Centre de Santé Sainte Bernadette. Les chiffres déroulés sont insoutenables et traduisent une courbe ascendante : 56 cas en 2023, 69 en 2024, 77 en 2025 et déjà 60 cas en septembre 2026. Une spirale meurtrière que les réseaux sociaux tentent de banaliser. Pour la Dr Soundjock Massé Flavie, organisatrice, il faut revenir à la base : "Quand on parle de féminicide, on a d'abord besoin de la vraie définition. Il faut qu'il y ait un lien. On a demandé aux femmes de se prendre en charge et de prévenir." Elle plaide pour une rééducation dès l'enfance dans le contexte africain, la vigilance face aux émotions et aux réseaux sociaux qui disent tout et son contraire, et surtout la bienveillance. "Fixer des bases dans nos relations", comme l'a rappelé un avocat présent. La table ronde a débouché sur un partenariat concret avec le Cabinet Miyondo. Désormais, les victimes de violences basées sur le genre, hommes ou femmes, pourront se référer au Centre Médical Sainte-Mélanie pour les soins, le volet juridique étant assuré par le cabinet. Prochaine étape : saisir l'État. Un rapport sera adressé aux ministères pour que le féminicide cesse d'être un fait divers et devienne une priorité de politique publique. Cet article Féminicide au Cameroun : les chiffres alarmants est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Londres : le Cameroun séduit les investisseurs
data.description: © DR Une délégation camerounaise conduite par le DG du CNCC, Auguste Mbappe Penda, participe depuis le 10 septembre 2026 à Londres à une réunion de haut niveau sur la gestion des risques et la résilience des entreprises. Aux côtés du Maire de Londres, Dame Susan Langley, Yaoundé entend capter de nouvelles opportunités d'investissement dans un contexte mondial incertain. Le Cameroun à l'offensive à la City. Une délégation d'hommes d'affaires et de responsables gouvernementaux séjourne à Londres pour une importante rencontre consacrée à la gestion des risques et au renforcement de la résilience des entreprises. Dans un contexte économique mondial marqué par l'instabilité, les discussions portent sur des enjeux cruciaux : santé, échanges transfrontaliers, pétrole et énergie, environnement et sécurité. La rencontre réunit autour du Maire de Londres, Dame Susan Langley, des délégations de Guernesey, d'Australie-Occidentale, du Togo et du Cameroun, ainsi que des multinationales de renom. Le Conseil National des Chargeurs du Cameroun occupe une place de choix. Son Directeur Général, Auguste Mbappe Penda, participe en tant que Chairman du Pôle régional du Commonwealth Enterprise and Investment Council pour le Cameroun, le Gabon, le Togo et la Sierra Leone. Une position stratégique qui permet de porter la voix du Cameroun et de l'Afrique centrale dans les cercles d'investissement du Commonwealth et d'explorer de nouvelles opportunités pour les entreprises camerounaises. Cet article Londres : le Cameroun séduit les investisseurs est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroun : Pierre Emmanuel Binyam, candidat pour succéder à Maurice Kamto au MRC
data.description: © (DR) Dans un message adressé aux militantes et militants du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun, le secrétaire général adjoint dévoile sa décision en précisant le contexte. Trois jours après la démission du Pr Maurice Kamto à la tête du MRC, le secrétaire général adjoint, Pierre Emmanuel Binyam, rend publique sa décision de lui succéder. À travers Facebook, le cadre du parti informe les militantes et militants de ce parti politique de sa décision de présenter sa candidature. Pour les élections qui auront lieu lors de la convention qui s’annonce au siège du parti à Yaoundé, le candidat déclaré dit avoir constitué son équipe. Sa liste est déjà prête. La candidature est annoncée au moment où le parti prépare la convention annoncée pour reconstituer la hiérarchie du parti à l'approche des échéances électorales. À la lecture du message du candidat, trois défis justifient son intention. La préparation des élections municipales et législatives de 2027, la recherche d'une majorité parlementaire et municipale, la consolidation des acquis du parti dans son combat pour l'Etat de droit et le changement. « Je souhaite ainsi contribuer au débat sur l'avenir, l'organisation et les orientations du MRC, dans le respect de ses principes et de ses valeurs », annonce-t-il. Pierre Emmanuel Binyam n'est pas un inconnu au MRC. Faisant partie du premier cercle dudit parti, le juriste de formation est l'un des cadres qui ont porté la formation politique pendant les périodes difficiles. En particulier après le placement en détention des membres du directoire en 2019 ainsi que lors du boycott des élections législatives et municipales en 2020. Il est l'un des acteurs qui maîtrisent la formation politique dans son fonctionnement interne. En se présentant pour la présidence du MRC, Pierre Binyam entend redonner au parti une nouvelle trajectoire à la suite du boycott des élections et de la fermeture du débat sur la succession à la tête de la formation politique. Il veut peser un peu plus sur la ligne politique en 2027 en progressent du poste de secrétaire adjoint vers une poste plus en vue. Il prend la posture de celui qui veut conquérir le siège occupé depuis plus d'une décennie par Maurice Kamto. Lui qui bénéficie d'un soutien populaire massif, a tenté en 2018 de succéder au président Paul Biya à la tête de l'État. Mais n'a récolté que 14% des suffrages au tableau des résultats officiels. Emmanuel Binyam peut compter sur sa connaissance de l'appareil MRC et sur le réseau des fédérations de la formation politique. Ainsi s'ouvre la succession à la présidence du MRC. Les prochains développements s'annoncent démocratiques. Cet article Cameroun : Pierre Emmanuel Binyam, candidat pour succéder à Maurice Kamto au MRC est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Restauration des terres au Cameroun : la BAD et la BID en renfort
data.description: © DR En marge de la COP17 sur la désertification à Oulan-Bator, le Cameroun a mobilisé la Banque Africaine de Développement et la Banque Islamique de Développement pour financer la restauration de 12 millions d'hectares de terres dégradées. Yaoundé joue sa diplomatie verte. En marge de la COP17 de la Convention des Nations unies sur la lutte contre la désertification, tenue à Oulan-Bator en Mongolie, le Cameroun a engagé des discussions décisives avec la BAD et la BID. Objectif : financer son ambitieux programme de restauration de 12 millions d'hectares de terres dégradées. Les échanges, qualifiés de fructueux, ont porté sur des leviers essentiels : résilience climatique, sécurité alimentaire, structuration des chaînes de valeur agricoles et création d'emplois pour les jeunes et les femmes en zone rurale. Pour Yaoundé, il s'agit d'un axe politique majeur. La dégradation des sols affecte plus de 60% des terres arables dans les régions septentrionales et menace directement la souveraineté alimentaire. De nouveaux mécanismes de financement sont envisagés pour accompagner le prochain Cadre de coopération des Nations unies pour le développement durable au Cameroun, avec l'appui technique de la CNULCD. Un signal fort qui confirme le positionnement du Cameroun comme acteur clé de la lutte contre la désertification en Afrique centrale. Cet article Restauration des terres au Cameroun : la BAD et la BID en renfort est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Sécurité alimentaire : l’IRAD déploie ses semences à Foumbot
data.description: © DR Le 10 septembre 2026 à Foumbot, l'IRAD a organisé une Journée portes ouvertes dédiée au maïs. Objectif : vulgariser les semences améliorées hybrides pour booster la production dans l'Ouest et lutter contre l'insécurité alimentaire, dans le cadre du programme TAAT financé par la BAD. Le maïs comme arme contre la faim. L'Institut de Recherche Agricole pour le Développement (IRAD) a organisé le 10 septembre 2026 à Foumbot, région de l'Ouest, une Journée Portes Ouvertes centrée sur la vulgarisation des semences améliorées. L'enjeu est stratégique : augmenter durablement la production céréalière dans le bassin agricole de l'Ouest, considéré comme grenier du pays, et répondre à l'insécurité alimentaire. L'accent a été mis sur les variétés hybrides à haut rendement, plus résistantes et adaptées aux changements climatiques. Cette activité s'inscrit dans le programme TAAT Compact Maïs, financé par la Banque Africaine de Développement (BAD), avec comme partenaires l'IRAD et la Fondation pour les Technologies Agricoles en Afrique (AATF). Pour le gouvernement, cette démarche traduit la volonté de passer d'une agriculture de subsistance à une agriculture de production, en mettant la recherche au service du paysan. Cet article Sécurité alimentaire : l’IRAD déploie ses semences à Foumbot est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
